Lessons.Title: Recalling Percent Change
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: express percentage increases and decreases as equivalent additive, distributive and single-multiplier forms, distinguishing retained amount from percentage amount and understanding the effect of successive percent changes. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of optional Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 14, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/14/preparation.html and student lesson https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/14/index.html (CC BY 4.0). This is a review of earlier percent-change reasoning, not falsely labelled a new publisher Addressing objective.

Original fictional starting price $200. A 15% rise gives $200+$30=$230, equivalently200×1.15. A 20% markdown gives $200−$40=$160, equivalently200×0.8. Two successive changes of +10% then−10% give200×1.1×.9=$198, not the original $200; the second percent uses a different base.

A change of r percent is a multiplier1+r/100 for an increase and1−r/100 for a decrease, when the changes refer to the CURRENT value. Multiplying by.2 yields20% of the original, while multiplying by.8 gives the retained amount after a20% reduction.

Student task: match three equivalent expressions for percent changes, identify a non-equivalent distractor, compute successive changes in two orders and explain why symmetrical nominal percents do not cancel multiplicatively. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for correct percent arithmetic, equivalent forms, base interpretation and critique of incorrect cancellation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Increase multiplier
KeyConcepts.Definition: Increasing by r% means multiplying by1+r/100.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decrease multiplier
KeyConcepts.Definition: Reducing by r% means retaining multiplier1−r/100.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compounded percentages
KeyConcepts.Definition: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors and generally do not cancel.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use current value for each change.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming equal+10% and−10% undo one another
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The two steps use different percentage bases.
The discount and sale price are different quantities.

SummaryPoints: Percent changes can be written with a single multiplicative factor.
An r% reduction retains1−r/100 of current amount.
Successive percentage changes compound rather than add simply.
Teacher checks explanation and equivalence rather than one answer.
